title: Two Shells Home: how I let an AI agent drive the Unity editor to build a zombie roguelite (bridge, UI generator, tests, Steam pipeline)
author: Zanoshky
selftext:

My first post here was only a link, and the mods rightly asked how AI was actually used. Fair point, so here is the whole process.

**The game.** Two Shells Home is a top down zombie survival roguelite. You hold a double barrel shotgun and walk home through a dark, misty forest. A run is five stages on an FTL style route map: you pick your way from camp to the house, trading risk for reward, and the Butcher waits at the end. Shells are always short, kills fill a level bar, and skill points buy nodes on a six branch skill tree. Getting home unlocks a perk for every run after.

**How AI was used**

* **An agent driving the Unity editor.** Claude Code writes the C#, but the bigger change was letting it use the editor itself. A small editor script (the "agent bridge") watches a command.json file every 0.4 s and runs what it finds: play, pause, open scene, screenshot, inspect an object, set a field, add a component, call any static method. The result and every log line go back into a result file. So the agent can change code, press Play, take a screenshot, read the console and fix what it sees, with nobody clicking.
* **A live profiler it can read.** In play mode a tiny runtime script writes frame times, spike frames, GC and draw calls to a JSON file every 3 s. The agent reads that instead of me describing "it feels laggy".
* **UI as code, not as clicks.** The card screen, the HUD additions and the death summary are built by an editor script, and a verify script fails if any reference is left empty. Everything the generator owns is rebuilt on each run. This was the biggest lesson: an agent (or me) tweaking those objects in the Inspector looks fine until the next rebuild silently wipes it. The script is the source of truth.
* **Data from tables.** The 27 upgrade cards are seeded from a table in an editor script. A rebuild only fills in missing cards, so numbers tuned by hand are kept.
* **Tests in batch mode.** 62 EditMode tests (camp, route map, run loop, roguelite, platform) run headless before every change is called done.
* **The Steam pipeline.** Python scripts written with the agent build the logo, store capsules, app icons and all 60 achievement icons. A batch mode run plays the game to capture the store screenshots, and the trailer is cut by a script from one session I recorded myself.

**What AI did not do.** The models, effects and UI kit are bought Unity asset packs, and the game ships no AI generated art. I decide what the game is, play every build, and say what is fun and what is not.

**Traps worth knowing if you try this**

* A batch tool that calls EditorApplication.Exit through the bridge makes the bridge replay the last command when the editor comes back: an endless loop. Keep those tools out of the bridge.
* Unity batch mode can fail when the Mac screen is locked.
* For staged screenshots, the line of sight system hid every zombie the player could not see, so the key art came out empty until the hiders were switched off for capture.
* Steamworks' achievement bulk import says every file succeeded but saves only the first 10. Upload 10 and save, per batch.

About 17,700 lines of C# in 89 scripts so far.

Steam: https://store.steampowered.com/app/5578490/

Happy to go deeper on the bridge or the UI generator if anyone wants to build something similar.
